newsitem.title: UK: Rifkind rules out change in UK stance on EMU.
newsitem.headline: Rifkind rules out change in UK stance on EMU.

text.p: Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind on Thursday ruled out any change in the British government's wait-and-see stance on whether to join the European Union's planned single currency.

He was speaking ahead of a discussion in cabinet of a briefing paper on monetary union that "Euro-sceptics" in the ruling Conservative party had hoped might prompt ministers to adopt an explicitly hostile line on the controversial question.
But Rifkind told BBC radio: "The cabinet has already come to a conclusion. I don't see any evidence that there's going to be a change."

He said the cabinet's decision last April to keep its options open on the single currency -- taking advantage of the opt-out secured by Prime Minister John Major when the project was agreed in 1991 -- was shared by the vast majority of Conservative members of parliament.
This was because it was clearly in Britain's interest not to decide now whether to sign up for the single currency, which is due to be launched on January 1, 1999.

"Does the national interest require a decision now? The answer is "no, it does not.' British influence would be diminished, and in any event decisions on this issue are going to be taken around about a year from now," Rifkind said.

He said the national interest was further protected because the Conservatives -- like the main opposition Labour party -- had promised to hold a referendum to endorse any future decision to scrap sterling in favour of the sinle currency.
"So the British public would always have the last word. Against that background the national interest is very clear and quite unmistakable," the Foreign Secretary said.
The paper, due to be discussed at Thursday's weekly cabinet meeting, has been drafted by finance minister Kenneth Clarke, the government's leading pro-European.
The report looks mainly at whether other European countries are "fudging" the criteria for entry into a single currency.

The paper was ordered before Christmas when Clarke came under pressure from ministers who wanted Major, behind in the polls and facing an election by May, should take a more sceptical stance on the single currency.
Rifkind confirmed he would be making a series of speeches to the people of Europe in coming weeks over the heads of their politicians to set out Britain's vision of a flexible, free-market Europe.
"The issue of the future of Europe doesn't just belong to the politicians. It doesn't just belong to diplomats," he said.

"We're talking about jobs, trade and the quality of life, and therefore it's right that the peoples of Europe -- better educated than ever before -- should be fully part of that debate," Rifkind added.
